newsitem.title: USA: U.S. House clears tax breaks for struggling D.C..
newsitem.headline: U.S. House clears tax breaks for struggling D.C..

text.p: The U.S. House on Thursday approved millions of dollars of tax breaks designed to reverse the flight of businesses and residents from the District of Columbia.
"This is absolutely historical," an aide to Virginia Republican Tom Davis, who chairs a House panel that oversees D.C. finances, said in a telephone interview during debate on the measure.
"All in all, this is a major success for the District," Office of Management and Budget Director Franklin Raines told reporters at a briefing.
The package, approved Thursday by the House, provides tax relief to businesses in poorer sections of the city that hire local residents.
Business owners would get a 20 percent tax break on the first $15,000 that they pay workers living and working in District neighborhoods with higher poverty rates, a summary of the plan says.
The plan also would wipe out capital gains taxes for businesses that make 80 percent of their income in areas of the city with a 10 percent poverty rate, the summary says.
And, it would provide a $5,000 tax credit for first-time homebuyers in the city.
The credit could be used by people that earn up to $70,000 a year and couples with combined yearly incomes of $130,000, the summary adds.
Behind its tourist attractions -- the White House, the monuments and the museums -- Washington is a troubled city with a rapidly shrinking population, mostly poor and black.
The number of D.C. residents has plummeted from 800,000 in 1950 to under 550,000 in 1997 as people flee in search of cheaper houses, less crime and competent schools.
Businesses have abandoned the city or refused to locate here because of some of the highest business taxes in the country.
D.C.'s delegate to Congress, Eleanor Holmes Norton, has warned that a continued loss of residents and companies will cripple D.C. for good.

The D.C. tax incentives proposal is part of a landmark measure to cut taxes for U.S. taxpayers and businesses a net $95 billion over five years that is moving rapidly toward final action by Congress and the White House.
